# Instructions

Your second write-up follows the same steps as the first, with one change: this time your question compares **three or more** groups or conditions, so you will run an **ANOVA** instead of a *t* test. Your group (2–3 people) will pick a new dataset, ask a question about three or more groups or conditions, state your hypotheses, run the ANOVA and post-hoc tests in R, and report what you found in APA style with a figure.

There are two kinds of ANOVA you can run, and **your dataset decides which one**:

| If your data have… | Run a… | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| **Different people** in each group (each person contributes one score) | **One-way between-groups ANOVA** | Lecture 15 (Nov. 17), Discussion 11 |
| **The same people** in every condition (each person contributes one score per condition) | **One-way repeated-measures ANOVA** | Lecture 16 (Nov. 19), Discussion 12 |

**This file is the assignment.** You will fill it in over two discussion sections and submit it once. Each part below says what goes in it and how it's graded.

| When | What you'll complete |
|---|---|
| Discussion 11 (Nov. 18) | Form groups and choose a dataset; Parts 1–3 (research question and hypotheses, *before* looking at the data); then start Part 4 |
| Before Discussion 12 | Finish Part 4 (descriptive statistics, histograms, assumption check) |
| Discussion 12 (Dec. 2) | Parts 5–7: run the ANOVA and post-hoc tests, make the figure, interpret |
| Tuesday, Dec. 8, 11:59 p.m. | Deadline |

**Remember:** decide your research question, variables, and hypotheses (Parts 1–3) *before* you look at the data. Once you've looked, don't rewrite Parts 2–3 to match the results.

**Datasets.** Choose one from the Data Write-Up #2 menu at the end of the Discussion 11 worksheet (course website → Discussion Section → Discussion 11). You must use a **different dataset** from the one you used in Write-Up #1. You can work in either the same group or a different group, but you must work in a group of 2 - 3 people. The **dataset card** for each one lists its columns, what one row represents, which kind of ANOVA it supports, and the source to cite. You may not use a dataset that isn't on the menu unless your TF has approved it in writing before Discussion 12.

**Group work.** Everyone in the group works on every part. Submit **one** file per group with all full names at the top via Slack to Kate and Rola. Work in this file on one person's computer (or share it), and keep the CSV in the same `ps211` project folder as this file. 

**Writing counts.** This is a report, not a worksheet. Write in complete sentences and proofread. We will check that your results follow **APA style exactly** (italic *F* and *p*, degrees of freedom in parentheses, no leading zero on *p* or η², and so on) and **typos will cost points**.

**AI and collaboration.** Per the syllabus, you may use AI tools and talk to people outside your group, but you must say so in the statement at the end of this file.

## Rubric (100 points)

| Part | What is graded | Points |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Dataset | Dataset named and cited; one-sentence description; what one row is; number of participants | 5 |
| 2. Question & variables | Clear, answerable research question; IV with its three or more levels; DV and its scale; which ANOVA (between-groups or repeated-measures) and why | 15 |
| 3. Hypotheses | Null and alternative hypotheses in words; a specific prediction about which group(s) will differ, with a reason; alpha | 10 |
| 4. Descriptives | *M*, *SD*, and *n* for every group or condition in a table; histograms; a few sentences on distribution shape for each group or condition and on whether the SDs are similar | 10 |
| 5. The test | Correct ANOVA run on the right data; *F*, both *df*, *p*, and η² (partial η² for repeated measures) reported in APA format; post-hoc tests reported | 20 |
| 6. Figure | One figure showing every group or condition mean with SE error bars, in a sensible order; labeled axes; a caption that says what the reader should see | 15 |
| 7. Interpretation | Decision about H0 in plain language; which groups differ; size of the effect in plain language; one design limitation and one sample limitation; a follow-up question | 15 |
| Code & writing | Every chunk runs and shows its output; code is commented; file knits; names at the top; proofread; APA formatting exact; AI/collaboration statement completed | 10 |

## How to submit

Knit this file to HTML (the **Knit** button) and send the `.html` file to Kate and Rola on Slack. **Each group submits exactly once: no resends.** The first file we receive from your group is the one we grade, so check it carefully before you send it. The deadline is **Tuesday, Dec. 8, at 11:59 p.m.** If knitting fails, the error message names the chunk; fix that chunk and knit again. A file that doesn't knit can't be graded. **Before you send it, open the HTML and check that your histograms and your figure appear in it.**

## If you see this error, it means…

- `'xxx.csv' does not exist` → R can't find your data file. Is it in your `ps211` folder, and is the project open?
- `object 'xxx' not found` → you used a name R doesn't know: usually a typo in a column name, or a chunk above this one hasn't been run yet. Check spelling and capitalization, then run the chunks from the top.
- A level shows up as `NA` in your descriptives table → a level name inside `levels = c(...)` doesn't match the data exactly. Copy it from the `count()` output.
- A level you didn't expect is in your table, or `n` is twice as big as it should be → you forgot a `filter()` step that your dataset card says you need (for example, choosing one time point or one task).
- `Error() model is singular` or the ANOVA table has only one section → you ran the repeated-measures code on data where each person appears only once. Check which kind of ANOVA your dataset supports.
- `pairwise.t.test` gives `not all arguments have the same length` → some participants are missing a condition. Tell your TF; the menu datasets shouldn't have any.
- Your plot shows the conditions in alphabetical order (e.g., `block_1`, `block_10`…) or in an order that makes no sense → set the order with `levels = c(...)` in Part 4.

# Part 5: Run your ANOVA (20 points)

*Complete in Discussion 12.*

Use **one** of the two code blocks below (leave the other commented), matching what you said in Part 2.

**Option A: one-way between-groups ANOVA** (different people in each group). `TukeyHSD()` then compares every pair of groups while keeping the overall chance of a Type I error at alpha (Lecture 15).

```{r part5-between}
# Remove the # signs and run:
# anova_result <- aov(dv ~ iv, data = my_data)
# summary(anova_result)
# TukeyHSD(anova_result)
```

**Option B: one-way repeated-measures ANOVA** (the same people in every condition). `Error(participant/iv)` tells R that each participant was measured in every condition, so R can remove the variability due to individual differences (Lecture 16). The post-hoc tests are paired *t* tests for every pair of conditions, with a Bonferroni correction.

```{r part5-repeated}
# Remove the # signs and run:
# my_data$participant <- factor(my_data$participant)   # participant IDs must be a factor, not numbers
# my_data <- arrange(my_data, iv, participant)          # same participant order in every condition, for the paired tests
# anova_result <- aov(dv ~ iv + Error(participant/iv), data = my_data)
# summary(anova_result)
# pairwise.t.test(my_data$dv, my_data$iv, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")
```

**Effect size.** Compute the effect size yourself from the sums of squares in your `summary()` output (Lectures 15–16). It is the proportion of variability explained by your IV:

- Between-groups: η² = *SS*~IV~ / (*SS*~IV~ + *SS*~Residuals~), which is *SS*~Between~ / *SS*~Total~.
- Repeated-measures: report **partial η²**. Use the **lower** section of the output (`Error: participant:iv`): partial η² = *SS*~IV~ / (*SS*~IV~ + *SS*~Residuals~). This leaves *SS*~Subjects~ (the upper section) out of the denominator, as in Lecture 16.

```{r part5-eta-squared}
# Copy the two Sum Sq values from your ANOVA table:
# SS_iv  <- ___
# SS_res <- ___
# eta_sq <- SS_iv / (SS_iv + SS_res)
# eta_sq
```

**Report the result in APA style.** Two to four sentences: say which ANOVA you ran, then report *F*(*df*~IV~, *df*~Residuals~), *p*, and η² (or partial η²), then the post-hoc tests with the means and SDs of the groups that differed. If your ANOVA is not significant, report it the same way and skip the post-hoc sentence.

WRITE YOUR APA RESULTS PARAGRAPH HERE.

#### Rubric
- 6 points: the right ANOVA for the design, run on the right rows, with the right post-hoc tests.
- 4 points: η² (or partial η²) computed correctly from the sums of squares.
- 8 points: APA paragraph correctly reports *F*, both *df*, *p*, η² or partial η², and the post-hoc results with *M* and *SD*, in exact APA format.
- 2 points: code runs and is commented.

**Caption.** Write two or three sentences under the figure. This should include: what is plotted, what the error bars represent, and what the reader should notice. For a repeated-measures design, note that these error bars show how much each condition's mean would vary from sample to sample; they include the differences *between people*, which the repeated-measures ANOVA removes, so they can overlap even when the ANOVA is significant.
